content: Tinospora cordifolia, commonly referred to as Guduchi, is a climbing herbaceous vine belonging to the Menispermaceae family. It is native to tropical regions of India, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka. This plant is known by various names in different languages, such as amrita in Sanskrit, giloe or giloya in Hindi, gulancha in Bengali, gado or galo in Gujarati, and duyutige or teppatige in Telugu. In English, it is sometimes called heartleaf moonseed. According to the 1911 British Pharmaceutical Codex, Tinospora cordifolia, also referred to as Gulancha, is derived from the dried stem of the plant. The stems are harvested during the hot season and then dried. The dried stems are typically cylindrical, either straight or twisted, and are available in pieces averaging about 2 centimeters in diameter, though smaller fragments are also common. The outer surface of the stem is covered with a thin, papery, brown cork layer, which features raised scars from numerous lenticels. This cork layer can easily peel off, revealing a greenish cortex beneath, which is longitudinally wrinkled and also marked with lenticels. When broken, the stem exhibits a fibrous texture. A cross-sectional view of the stem reveals yellowish wood with radially arranged, wedge-shaped wood bundles containing large vessels, separated by narrower medullary rays. The plant material has no distinctive odor but possesses a bitter taste. Chemical Constituents The plant contains several active adaptogenic compounds, including diterpenes such as tinosporone, tinosporic acid, and cordifolisides A to E. Other notable constituents include syringen, the yellow alkaloid berberine, and a glucosidal bitter principle known as Giloin. Additionally, it contains crude Giloininand and polysaccharides, such as arabinogalactan polysaccharide (TSP). Ethnobotanical and Medicinal Uses As documented in the 1918 edition of the United States Dispensatory, Tinospora cordifolia has been traditionally used in India for medicinal purposes and in the preparation of a starch known as gilae-ka-sat or palo. The plant is reputed to have tonic, antiperiodic (used to prevent recurring fevers), and diuretic properties. Flückiger, a researcher, identified traces of an alkaloid and a bitter glucoside in the plant. The British Addendum of 1900 recognized several pharmaceutical preparations of Tinospora cordifolia. These included: Infusion (Infusum Tinosporae): Prepared using two ounces of the plant material per pint of liquid. The recommended dosage was 15–30 milliliters (one-half to one fluid ounce). Tincture (Tinctura Tinosporae): Prepared using four ounces of the plant material per pint of liquid. The recommended dosage was 1.8–3.75 milliliters (one-half to one fluidrachm). Concentrated Solution: Specific details of the preparation were not provided, but it was another recognized form of administration.
